stories.headline: Levent Alpöge claims an AI-built proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, plus Navier-Stokes and Euler blow-up results in Lean
stories.why_read: The two biggest threads on Hacker News overnight, with more than 2,600 points: physics and math from your pinned post, colliding head-on with AI.
body: Levent Alpöge posted a short remark claiming a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis that, he writes, extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, discovered while "working with Claude" and formalized "without assumptions." He describes guiding the work toward the right setting and then watching the model "far outpace" him near the finish line. Terence Tao's same-day roundup describes it as an enormous, Lean-only proof generated with an internal AI model, and the least digested of the day's results.

Tao ranks two companion results as further along: a human-readable, Lean-formalized proof of finite-time blow-up for the unforced 3D incompressible Euler equations by Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster and Matei Coiculescu, and a proof of blow-up for the unforced 3D Navier-Stokes equations by Alpöge and Buckmaster, both built with heavy AI assistance. Formal verification is the reason people are taking this seriously instead of laughing it off, but Tao is explicit that the community still has to digest all of it.

stories.headline: Cursor is getting renamed Grok Build, with a faster app and Grok Build CLI 2.0 in alpha
stories.why_read: You retweeted both halves of this thread, and it is the tool you build with every day: new name, same cube, and a bundle tied to the unified subscription you bought.
body: Grok Insider reports that Cursor is being renamed Grok Build: "A new name, and a faster app." The post says Grok Build CLI 2.0 is already in an alpha unified channel, which suggests it will be tied to the unified X, Grok and Cursor subscription. Its one-line summary: "The cube stays. The Cursor name doesn't."

The follow-up lists what the announcement promises: a lighter, faster app on desktop and web; Projects, where a team of agents works on one big problem; one Project shared with your whole team, even from Slack; cloud agents you steer from your phone; and Grok, Anthropic, OpenAI and more models in one app.

stories.headline: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a looped open-weights model that runs on a laptop
stories.why_read: An open-weights model under 100B parameters that leads its class on agentic coding, and a new architectural trick worth understanding.
body: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini, a mixture-of-experts model with 26.4B total parameters and 3.4B active. It is a looped transformer: the middle layers run three times for every token, so the model can reason more without writing more tokens. The lab says it leads every open-weights model under 100B total parameters on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%), and runs faster than similarly performing models.

The interesting tension is monitorability. Looping lets a model think longer without writing its reasoning down, which makes chain-of-thought oversight harder, so the lab is also releasing a research variant with a variable number of loops to study that trade-off. It is available on Tinker and Hugging Face.

stories.headline: A second, all-human GRH proof gets a hurried announcement, and AI models quickly flag problems
stories.why_read: The same day as the AI-built claim, Ravi Vakil rushed out news of a human proof Brian Conrad has studied for months. Then the AI reviewers showed up.
body: Stanford's Ravi Vakil posted, between AMS board meetings, that Alessandro Maria Masullo has a proposed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. Brian Conrad has been examining it closely for months and gave extensive feedback, and Vakil stressed that "It is all human, with no AI." The plan had been a year of polishing before any announcement.

About eight hours later Vakil added an update: several people had reported problems in the proposed proof, identified with the help of different AI models. He noted that all issues must be resolved to the community's satisfaction before it could be accepted. It is a striking snapshot of where math is right now: AI on both sides of the proof-and-check loop.

stories.headline: Nasdaq erases its 2026 gains as the AI sell-off dampens Anthropic's second day
stories.why_read: You retweeted Dan Ives' six-part explanation and bookmarked Kobeissi's "-$6 trillion in 45 days" piece: the bubble-or-opportunity debate is now the market.
body: The Guardian reports that the Nasdaq has given back all of its 2026 gains as an AI-led sell-off weighed on Anthropic's second day of trading. Tesla shares fell more than 7% on November 20 in the same slide, according to X's news summaries.

Dan Ives lists his "perfect storm": fears of an anti-AI, anti-datacenter Washington after the election, losing Jensen Huang as the leader of the AI revolution, China-driven regulatory worries across semis and memory, market-clearing events that triggered more selling, and Anthropic's successful IPO pulling liquidity from other tech names. The Kobeissi Letter frames the same moment as -$6 trillion in 45 days and asks whether it is a bubble or an opportunity.

stories.headline: Cybercab spotted testing across Phoenix, and Tesla's Tempe site is already set up for Robotaxi
stories.why_read: You bookmarked and retweeted Robotaxi Radar's map of sightings: city three looks close.
body: Robotaxi Radar collected Cybercab sightings across the Valley this fall: Scottsdale, Mesa, Chandler highways and south Phoenix near Sky Harbor. Tesla's Tempe site already shows parking and cleaning as open and ready for Robotaxi use, while Phoenix is still listed as "coming soon" from Tesla's Q2 deck.

Ryan Tanaka posted another Cybercab in Phoenix and asked the obvious question: "They've gotta be launching soon, right?!" After Austin and Dallas, Phoenix would put Cybercab directly into Waymo's oldest market.

stories.headline: Language models can rewrite their own weights, no gradients required
stories.why_read: A genuinely new idea on the HN front page: an open 27B model acts as its own optimizer and gets better on problems it never saw.
body: A new arXiv paper by Jiajun Fan and ten co-authors proposes "self-rewriting": an open 27B model is given its own weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, then diagnoses its failures and edits the weights behind them, with no gradients and no training run. The authors report that its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw.

It keeps improving across eight consecutive sessions by testing edits on practice problems and submitting only what works. The authors also show it repairing a damaged copy of itself without retraining. Earlier work had a frontier model edit a much smaller one; here the model edits itself.

stories.headline: Gemini 4 Neon wins over the builders: "the closest I've tested to Opus and Fable"
stories.why_read: You retweeted Theo's verdict and Mia's 100-page design stress test: the model everyone in your feed is switching to this week.
body: Theo posted a long video review with a short verdict: "Gemini 4 Neon is an incredible model." Mia asked it to generate 100 HTML files that look stunning with zero repetitive designs, and called it the closest she has tested to Opus and Fable, and the first Google model she can use without frustration.
Dax went with receipts instead of vibes, sharing his team's model usage from last week, since "people are always suspicious of model reviews."

stories.headline: pstack v0.15.46 prunes its skills and adds Gemini 4 Neon as a panel reviewer
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it, and it auto-updates in the Grok Bot setup you run every day.
body: Poteto shipped pstack v0.15.46 with lots of pruning, so skills are much shorter, and Gemini 4 Neon added as a panel reviewer. It auto-updates for Grok Bot and Cursor users; to change model routing, run /setup-pstack again.
A Japanese post you retweeted connects pstack's idea that code is the best memory with the advice not to keep ADRs and docs in the codebase, and weighs it against README-driven development.

stories.headline: An interactive, in-browser walkthrough of how LLMs actually work, built on Gemma
stories.why_read: You retweeted Paige Bailey's pointer: tokenization through tool use, all running live in your browser.
body: Paige Bailey shared Google Gemma's interactive explainer, which walks through how LLMs work under the hood, from tokenization and embeddings to attention, sampling and tool use, completely interactively in the browser.
It is a good link to send to anyone who wants intuition rather than a paper.

stories.headline: We promoted developers into architects without telling them
stories.why_read: Written for exactly your job title: when AI writes the code, knowing what each line costs is the new seniority.
body: Mani Doraisamy describes a vibe-coded logging routine in a Google Forms add-on that tried to fetch the user's email, then the user ID, then logged an error, with each one-line call quietly making multiple API calls to Google. Because it ran first after install, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load.

His point: an architect would have logged just a timestamp, or moved the lookup off the critical path, and talked to marketing about the trade-off. With AI writing code, every developer is now making architectural decisions, whether or not anyone told them.

stories.headline: Dallas Robotaxi zone grows to 82 square miles as early Cybercab riders report sub-5-minute waits
stories.why_read: You retweeted Ethan McKanna's ride report from Tesla's second Cybercab city.
body: Tesla expanded its Dallas Robotaxi zone to about 82 square miles, adding a northeast section along North Central Expressway that includes The Hill Supercharger for easier fleet charging, according to X's news summary. The zone started at 31 square miles in April.
Ethan McKanna says Cybercab in Dallas is "working flawlessly" with sub-five-minute waits and perfect driving so far, and that he is seeing a ton of them on the road.

stories.headline: Tesla Robotaxi highway access coming soon?
stories.why_read: You retweeted Sawyer Merritt's teaser: highways are what turn a robotaxi from a neighborhood shuttle into airport runs.
body: Sawyer Merritt quoted a post hinting that Tesla Robotaxi may soon be allowed on highways, asking "Tesla robotaxi highway access coming soon?"
Robotaxi Radar's Phoenix post already logged Cybercab sightings on Chandler highways, so the testing appears to be underway.

stories.headline: Tesla sends invites for its 2026 annual shareholder meeting at Giga Texas on December 3
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: an Austin event two weeks out, with a possible SpaceX tie-up in the background.
body: Sawyer Merritt reports that Tesla has started sending invites to its 2026 annual shareholder meeting at Giga Texas on December 3.
X's news summaries note special committees are already exploring a potential Tesla-SpaceX deal that would need shareholder approval, which makes this year's meeting more interesting than usual.

stories.headline: Tesla's 7-million-square-foot Optimus factory at Giga Texas will apparently use Giga Presses
stories.why_read: You retweeted Sawyer's catch from Joe Tegtmeyer's drone footage of the build site down the road from you.
body: Sawyer Merritt points out that Tesla's new 7 million square foot Optimus factory at Giga Texas looks set to use Giga Presses, quoting Joe Tegtmeyer's footage of the site.
Separately, new close-ups of Optimus's hands show exposed boards and wiring, and Musk said he expects the robot to handle full dishwashing in 12 to 18 months, per X's news summary.

stories.headline: Marques Brownlee honors his 2024 Cybercab bet with a deposit in Austin
stories.why_read: You bookmarked and retweeted it: a famously skeptical reviewer putting $1,000 down, and picking your city.
body: Marques Brownlee said he will "honor the spirit of the bet" he made in 2024. He was invited to buy a Cybercab, submitted a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and selected Austin, Texas.
If Tesla tells him his Cybercab is ready, he says, he will fly down to Austin to get it.

stories.headline: Valkey replaces the skiplist with a B+ tree and cuts sorted-set overhead by up to 43%
stories.why_read: A clean systems deep dive: why a classic data structure lost to cache-friendly contiguous memory.
body: In Valkey 9.2, large sorted sets are no longer backed by a skiplist. The team built fbtree, a high-fanout B+ tree variant with SIMD searches, linked leaves and fast paths for sequential inserts and pops. In a 5-million-member test it reduced per-member memory overhead by 36 to 43%, saving up to 109 MB.

The post breaks down why: a skiplist stores one element per node in scattered allocations, with a backward pointer plus an average of 1.33 levels of forward pointers and span values, which adds up to around 29 bytes of overhead per member before the data itself.

stories.headline: Vibecoding an inference chip: getting an FPGA to run an LLM with coding agents
stories.why_read: Inference hardware plus AI coding tools, two of your beats in one hands-on story.
body: Ankit Gupta knew little about FPGAs, so he pointed coding agents and a large token budget at one and tried to get it running an LLM. He recounts a series of "oh shit" moments, and says it just worked.
His larger point: coding agents let you work in entirely new domains, and low-level hardware is now one of them.

stories.headline: DreamCoder: a GUI-first AI coding harness from the author of Mastering Emacs
stories.why_read: A thoughtful counterpoint to terminal-first agents, from someone who has used Claude Code since its first week.
body: Mickey Petersen spent fifteen months building DreamCoder, an AI coding harness and IDE that he says is very different from the ones you know. He installed Claude Code days after its 2025 release and was struck by the speed, but also by the odd choice of a terminal as the primary interface.
His complaint: why stare at a shoe-rack-sized terminal window, when most GUI versions are second-class citizens? DreamCoder is his answer.

stories.headline: Critical GPGME bug: a crafted OpenPGP user ID triggers a double free; patch now
stories.why_read: Update notice for anyone who signs commits or mail: Werner Koch says RCE "can't be ruled out."
body: GnuPG released GPGME 2.3.1 to fix a critical bug in all prior versions (CVE-2026-129975). An OpenPGP key with a crafted, very long user ID can trigger a double free that could be used to exfiltrate data from applications, and remote code execution can't be ruled out. New Gpg4win and GnuPG Desktop builds ship the fix.
Johan Carlsson found it and GitLab reported it on November 12. Disclosure was moved up from November 25 because of a separate bug that forced GitLab to update early.

stories.headline: Inside Starfactory: one Starship upper stage every two weeks, a booster every four
stories.why_read: The follow-through on Flight 15's tower catch: production rate is now the story.
body: After Flight 15, where Ship 42 reached orbit, deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites and became the first upper stage caught by the tower, X's news summary reports that teams inside Starfactory now build one upper stage every two weeks and a booster every four.
The booster from that flight splashed down in the Gulf after an automated abort, and debris washed up on a beach in Mexico, which SpaceX says it is clearing.

stories.headline: Lenders on a $44 billion Nvidia Vera Rubin deal want SpaceX's chips kept on Earth
stories.why_read: Orbital compute meets credit risk: you cannot repossess a GPU in orbit.
body: Lenders behind a roughly $44 billion financing of Nvidia Vera Rubin GPUs leased to SpaceX want legal clauses preventing the chips from being launched into space, because repossession and resale on default would be impossible in orbit, according to X's news summary.
SpaceX says these chips stay in U.S. ground data centers, even as it eyes orbital compute projects starting in late 2027.

stories.headline: Cameron County halts a tax break for SpaceX's $24 billion Starbase data center and gas plant
stories.why_read: Data centers, power plants and Texas politics: the same anti-datacenter mood Dan Ives flagged, at county level.
body: Cameron County commissioners voted 3-2 to halt a public hearing on a 10-year, 100% property tax abatement for SpaceX's proposed $24 billion data center and natural gas power plant at Starbase, per X's news summary. The project promises 500 permanent jobs on 444 acres near Brownsville.
It already has its air permit and can proceed without the incentive.

stories.headline: The West faces a shortfall of about 150 medium and heavy launches through 2030
stories.why_read: Why Starship cadence matters beyond SpaceX: everyone else's rockets are behind.
body: U.S. and European launch capacity is short about 150 medium- and heavy-lift flights through 2030, per X's news summary, driven by SpaceX scaling back Falcon 9 rideshares after 2028, a recent Vulcan failure that lost 40 Amazon satellites, and delays at rivals like New Glenn.
Proposed fixes include pushing Falcon 9 to 100 to 150 launches a year and Space Force backing for a Starship spaceport.

stories.headline: Dragon heads home with bioprinted blood vessels and tumor organoids from the ISS
stories.why_read: Quiet science: what actually comes back on a cargo return.
body: SpaceX's Dragon undocked from the ISS on November 20 after 36 days and more than 6,300 pounds of deliveries, per X's news summary. It carries 3D-bioprinted blood vessels for heart disease studies, frozen tumor organoids for cancer research, and samples of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
The capsule will splash down off California.

stories.headline: Sir Brian May turns Hera's views of the Didymos asteroid into 3D
stories.why_read: Physics, astronomy and a rock star: a delightful one.
body: Astrophysicist and Queen guitarist Sir Brian May, a member of ESA's Hera science team, built stereoscopic images of the Didymos asteroid from two frames Hera captured on November 6 at 29.7 km with 2.8 m per pixel resolution.

In depth, he says, the sharpness of Didymos's equatorial ridge stands out against the rock-strewn surface. Principal investigator Patrick Michel says the 3D view makes the team feel like they are there, even from 197 million km away.

stories.headline: Neuralink: a patient plays GTA VI with his thoughts, and Blindsight awaits approval
stories.why_read: Human-interest and hard tech: from a mouth stick to two joysticks and 12 buttons.
body: Elon Musk shared a video of a Neuralink participant controlling the newly launched GTA VI with full PlayStation-style inputs decoded from over 1,000 neural channels, per X's news summary. Before the implant he used a mouth stick for his iPad.

Musk also described Blindsight, which sends camera signals directly to the visual cortex to create light patterns called phosphenes. It has FDA Breakthrough Device designation from 2024 and could help anyone with an intact visual cortex.

stories.headline: Nearly 1,000 AI agents ran independent research and invented their own peer review
stories.why_read: A glimpse of agent swarms doing science, with the self-correction built in.
body: Per X's news summary, the agents produced 936 studies with code, data and model weights, exchanged 9,500 messages across 229 rooms, and reported negative results more often than human preprints do.
They founded a Journal of Agent Research, where automated checks overturned nearly half of challenged claims, and publicly retracted errors.

stories.headline: Starlink kits help Ebola responders in Congo and connect 800 remote schools in Paraguay
stories.why_read: The love-and-kindness slot: connectivity where it saves lives and opens classrooms.
body: Africa CDC donated Starlink kits to frontline teams in Beni, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, speeding surveillance, case reporting and logistics during the country's 17th Ebola outbreak, according to X's news summary.
In Paraguay, SpaceX provided 1,600 kits that have connected 800 remote schools so far, including Indigenous communities in the Chaco, with another 400 on the way and hospitals planned.

stories.headline: Darren Shepherd open-sources his software factory built on discobox and skills
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: a real agent factory you can point your own agent at and ask how it works.
body: Darren Shepherd says his software factory is built on discobox and skills, and published the repos, discobox-ai/factory-demo and discobox-ai/manager, suggesting you ask your agent to explain what is in them.
Warp, also in your retweets, launched the first two units of its learning series at warp.dev/learn.
